title: Jitendra Desai — Principal hearing (2026-06-24)
text:
1

General Pharmaceutical Council
Fitness to Practise Committee
Principal Hearing
Remote videolink hearing
24 June 2026 – 2 July 2026

Registrant name:

Jitendra Desai
Registration number:

2048785
Part of the register:

Pharmacist
Type of Case:
Misconduct

Committee Members:

Manuela Grayson (Chair)

Jignesh Patel (Registrant member)

Joanne Hird (Lay member)

Committee Secretary:

Ivana Raimundova, Adam Hern

Registrant:
Not present and not represented
General Pharmaceutical Council:

Gareth Thomas, Case Presenter

Facts proved: 2.1, 2.2, 2.3, 3.1, 3.2 – including Schedule A
Facts not proved:

1.1, 1.2

Fitness to practise:

Impaired

Outcome:
Suspension Order for a period of 12 months
Interim measures:
Interim measure of suspension imposed

This decision including any ﬁnding of facts, impairment and sanction is an appealable decision under
The General Pharmaceutical Council (Fitness to Practise and Disqualiﬁcation etc. Rules) Order of Council

2

2010. Therefore, this decision will not take eﬀect until 31 July 2026 or, if an appeal is lodged, once that
appeal has been concluded. However, the interim suspension set out in the decision takes eﬀect
immediately and will lapse when the decision takes eﬀect or once any appeal is concluded.

3

Particulars of Allegation (as amended)

“You, a registered pharmacist, being the Responsible Pharmacist at Oakley Pharmacy,
270 Telegraph Road, Heswall, Wirral CH60 7SE (“the pharmacy”),

1. Between January 2023 and October 2023, failed to:
1.1 keep an up-to-date Responsible Pharmacist record
1.2 have in place and/or keep up to date a controlled drugs register when you knew or
ought to have known that the pharmacy was dispensing controlled drugs
[NOT PROVED]

2. On or around 27 September 2024, you attended work whilst unﬁt in that you:
2.1 slurred your speech;
2.2 were unsteady on your feet;
2.3 had consumed alcohol.
[PROVED]

3. On, or around 12 December 2024, disposed of an unknown quantity of medication and
conﬁdential pharmacy waste detailed in Schedule A, in an unsafe manner in or around
Beacon Park, Heswell, Wirral Council in that you:
3.1 failed to de-nature the medications or otherwise render them safe prior to disposal
3.2 discarded the medication and / or conﬁdential pharmacy waste in waste bags.
[PROVED]

By reasons of matters set out above, your ﬁtness to practise is impaired by reasons of your misconduct.

Schedule A
1. Mr W GPhC Inspector business card – exhibit CW/03
2. E-mail print out between Ms Islam, GPhC Case Oﬃcer and the Registrant – exhibit
CW/04
3. Four pages of near miss records – exhibit CW/05 to CW/07
4. 1 x Eumovate cream tube;

4

5. 1 x Ketoconazole cream tube;
6. 1 x Hydrocortisone cream tube;
7. 21 x Nicorette 4mg gum;
8. 15 x Piriton 4mg tablets;
9. 19 x Finasteride 1mg tablets;
10. 4 x Loratadine 10mg tablets;
11. 20 x Amoxicillin 500mg capsules;
12. 13 x Flucloxacillin 500mg capsules;
13. 17 x Omeprazole 20mg capsules;
14. 4 x Zolpidem 10mg tablets;
15. 7 x Lorazepam 2.5mg tablets”.

5

Documentation
At Stage 1 (Facts):
Document 1- GPhC hearing bundle, 183 pages
Document 2- Additional Bundle, 21 pages
Document3- GPhC skeleton argument, 14 pages, dated 17 June 2026
Document 4- Proof of Service bundle, 7 pages
Document 5- Proceeding In Absence bundle, 21 pages
Document 6- Notice of hearing dated 13 May 2026
Document 7- Bundle of documents received on ﬁrst day of hearing including emails from Registrant
dated 23 and 24 June 2026; two medical Fit notes from Registrant; ﬁle note of Committee Secretary,
Ms Raimundova, dated 24 June 2026
Document 8- 24 June 2026 email sent to Registrant by Committee Secretary informing him that the
hearing would proceed in his absence
Document 9- bundle of documentation provided by the Council on 29 June 2026, including
documentation from Council’s register; from Companies House; emails from the Registrant
demonstrating which CD register records were attached.
At Stage 2 (Impairment):
Documents 10,11 and 12: FTP Committee Determination from September 2019 (Principal Hearing);
FTP Committee Determination from March 2023 (Principal Hearing Review); FTP Committee
Determination from May 2025 (Interim Order Review).
At Stage 3 (Outcome):
Document 13: Documentation about the Warning imposed by the Investigating Committee in 2012

Witnesses:
Dr M, then GP Partner, Myrtle Group Practice
Dr W, GP Partner, Myrtle Group Practice
Ms K, then Practice Manager, Myrtle Group Practice
Mr L, then GPhC Inspector
Mr O, then locum pharmacist, Oakley pharmacy
Mr W, GPhC Inspector, pharmacist

6

Determination

Introduction
1.
This is the written determination of the Fitness to Practise Committee at the General
Pharmaceutical Council (‘the Council’).
2.
The hearing is governed by The Pharmacy Order 2010 (“the Order”) and The General
Pharmaceutical Council (Fitness to Practise and Disqualiﬁcation etc. Rules) Order of Council
2010 (“the Rules”).
3.
The statutory overarching objectives for these regulatory proceedings are:
a. To protect, promote and maintain the health, safety and well-being of the public;
b. To promote and maintain public conﬁdence in the professions regulated by the Council;
and
c. To promote and maintain proper professional standards and conduct for members of
those professions.

4.
The Committee also has regard to the guidance contained in the Council’s Good decision
making: Fitness to practise hearings and outcomes guidance as revised March 2024.
5.
A Principal Hearing has up to three stages:
Stage 1. Findings of Fact – the Committee determines any disputed facts.
Stage 2. Findings of ground(s) of impairment and impairment – the Committee
determines whether, on the facts as proved, a statutory ground for impairment is
established and, if so, whether the Registrant’s ﬁtness to practise is currently impaired.
Stage 3. Outcome – the Committee considers what, if any, outcome or sanction should be
applied if the Registrant’s ﬁtness to practise is found to be impaired.

Service of Notice of Hearing
6.
The Committee was provided with the Council’s “Proof of Service” bundle. It contained a
letter dated 13 May 2026 from the Council headed ‘Notice of Hearing’ addressed to the
Registrant. The Committee observed evidence in the bundle which showed that the Notice
was sent to the Registrant’s email address as it appears on the register, and that the
Registrant had consented to documentation being sent by the Council to his registered email

7

address. The Committee was satisﬁed that there had been good service of the Notice in
accordance with Rules 3 and 16.

Application to Proceed in the Absence of the Registrant
7.
The Registrant was not in attendance at this hearing, nor was someone attending on his
behalf.

8.
The Committee heard submissions from Mr Thomas on behalf of the Council, to proceed in
the absence of the Registrant in accordance with Rule 25, and with relevant case law
including the case of GMC v Hayat [2018] EWCA Civ 2796. Mr Thomas informed the
Committee that the Registrant had not been in contact with the Council at all for about a year
until about 10pm on the evening of 23 June 2026, when the Registrant wrote to the
Committee Secretary, Ms Raimundova, in response to her email to him containing the link for
this remote hearing.

9.
Mr Thomas submitted that the Registrant could have engaged with these proceedings at any
time before that but had not done so.

10.
Mr Thomas further submitted that there are at least six witnesses warned to take part in the
hearing, plus three others who may be called to give evidence, and all other arrangements,
for example convening the Committee, had been made for this listing. There was a public
interest in proceeding with the case as listed and the regulator’s overarching purpose, namely
public protection and protection of the public interest should be borne in mind by the
Committee when making its decision whether to proceed. Mr Thomas also drew the
Committee’s attention to the principles set out in the above case of Hayat regarding the
weight which can be given to GP ﬁt notes.

11.
The Committee considered all of the evidence relevant to whether it should proceed in the
Registrant’s absence.

8

12.
Evidence within the Council’s Proceeding in Absence bundle showed that after some
reminding from the Council, in early 2025, the Registrant had provided signed consent
documentation so that the Council could (REDACTED) but would respond that afternoon or
the following day, and thereafter he ceased to engage with the process.

13.
The evidence showed that all post in connection with this hearing sent to the Registrant’s
registered postal address was returned unopened; ‘egress’ emails sent to his registered email
address were not accessed; and those and other non-security-controlled emails were not
responded to. Private investigators were engaged by the Council twice during the
investigation period, to ascertain whether the Registrant was still living at the registered
address.

14.
The Registrant did not engage with the process after June 2025 until the email referred to
above, sent around 10pm on 23 June 2026.

15.
The Committee had agreed to delay the start of the hearing on 24 June 2026 so that Mr
Thomas and/or the Committee Secretary Ms Raimundova could speak to the Registrant to
ascertain his position with regard to whether to proceed, and whether he wished to take
part.

16.
The Committee was shown a ﬁle note prepared by Ms Raimundova following her phone call
with the Registrant on the morning of 24 June 2026. Ms Raimundova recorded as follows:

“I asked him if he had any implication (REDACTED)
I asked [him] whether he would like to attend in the future i.e. request a postponement but he
didn’t know when he could attend”.

17.
The Registrant said he had not accessed any documentation and had not seen the Particulars
of Allegation. Ms Raimundova suggested he speak to Mr Thomas.

9

18.
Following his conversation with Mr Thomas, in which, Mr Thomas told the Committee, the
Registrant said (REDACTED) and could not take part in the hearing, the Registrant sent the
following email message at 11.22:
“(REDACTED”.

19.
(REDACTED)

20.
In an email timed at 12.40 on 24 June 2026, the Registrant wrote to Mr Thomas in the
following terms:

“I would just like to say that all the allegations were due to (REDACTED)”.

21.
Having fully taken into account the contents of the Council’s Proceeding in Absence bundle,
and all of the further evidence of recent communications with the Registrant summarised
above, the Committee decided to proceed with the hearing in the absence of the Registrant
for the following reasons:

• The Committee has found good service of notice and the Registrant is aware of
today’s proceedings.
• The evidence before it is that the Registrant has engaged erratically at best with these
regulatory proceedings: he ceased communication in around June 2025; all attempts
to engage with him since then had been unsuccessful until he contacted Ms
Raimundova, the Committee Secretary, late on the evening before the hearing was
due to commence.
• The Committee considered (REDACTED)
• The Committee considered (REDACTED)
• Whilst the Registrant had also stated that a postponement would give him time to
“prepare [his] case” or “(REDACTED)” the Committee was bound to observe that he
had had ample opportunities over the year to access the documentation sent to him
both by registered post and by secured encrypted email, and then to engage with the

10

process and prepare his case, but he had not done so. He had told the Committee
Secretary that he had not even read the Particulars of Allegation.
• It appeared to the Committee, after carefully considering the recent communications
with the Registrant, that although he had, on the morning the hearing was due to
commence, made a request for a three- month postponement, he had been unable to
provide any independent evidence to suggest that (REDACTED).
• The Committee is of the view, taking all of the above into account, that it cannot be
assured that postponing the hearing and arranging a new listing in future would result
in the Registrant’s attendance.
• There were six witnesses ready to provide live evidence; and three more on stand- by
who might be required as well; postponement on the ﬁrst day of the listing with the
expectation that they will be asked to participate at a future date could cause them
considerable inconvenience.
• The allegations were serious and date from alleged events some years ago; given the
regulator’s overriding purpose as set out above, it is in the public interest for
proceedings to take place expeditiously.

22.
The Committee appreciated that the Registrant could be disadvantaged by this hearing
proceeding in his absence and without representation however the Committee resolved to
mitigate any risk by carefully examining any inconsistencies in the Council’s case and at all
times during its deliberations and during the hearing, bearing in mind that the Registrant is
absent.

Applications on behalf of the Council to amend the Particulars of Allegation
23.
At the start of the hearing, the Committee heard an application from Mr Thomas on behalf of
the Council under Rule 41 to amend the Particulars of Allegation by adding the following:

“2.3: had consumed alcohol”.

24.
Mr Thomas submitted that the Registrant had been notiﬁed of the Council’s intention to
amend the Allegation as above by email on 10 June 2026, but he had not responded. Mr

11

Thomas submitted that the amendment would not be unfair to the Registrant but would
better particularise the facts.

25.
Mr Thomas reminded the Committee that whilst fairness to the Registrant was important,
there was also a duty to be fair to the regulator and the wider public interest.

26.
The Committee was of the view that the Registrant had been given suﬃcient notice of the
proposed amendment. It agreed that there was some evidence which it would need to assess
in due course in relation to whether the Registrant had, on the relevant date, consumed
alcohol. It was satisﬁed that this amendment would not prejudice the fairness of the
proceedings.

27.
Accordingly, the Committee accepted the amendment to add the Council’s proposed
particular 2.3 to the Particulars of Allegation proposed on the behalf of the Council.

28.
After the evidence on behalf of the Council had been heard and before closing his case in
relation to the facts, Mr Thomas made a further application to amend the Particulars of
Allegation. He submitted that on the basis of all of the evidence now available, the Council
was not in a position to sustain an argument that the Registrant was the owner of the
Pharmacy. He provided a further bundle of evidence on behalf of the Council including screen
shots from the Council’s database, evidence from Companies House, and various evidence
from witnesses. He submitted that although the evidence was that a number of people,
including some employed at the Pharmacy and also staﬀ who worked next door at the GP
surgery thought or assumed that the Registrant owned the Pharmacy, this could not be
demonstrated in any documentation.

29.
Mr Thomas submitted that it would better reﬂect the evidence therefore to delete

“Owner and”

12

from the stem or preamble of the Allegation. He submitted that this would have the overall
eﬀect of reducing the gravity of the allegations so would not unfairly prejudice the Registrant.

30.
The Committee had regard to Rule 41 which allowed for it to amend the particulars “at any
stage before making its ﬁndings of fact”, unless it was of the view that the required
amendment would prejudice the fairness of the proceedings. Having carefully considered the
evidence available, the Committee agreed that this amendment better reﬂected the available
evidence as to whether the Registrant was the “owner” of the Pharmacy, and it considered
that the amendment would be likely to have the overall eﬀect of diminishing the gravity of
the concerns raised against the Registrant. For these reasons the Committee was satisﬁed
that the proposed amendment would not prejudice the fairness of the proceedings, and it
therefore accepted Mr Thomas’s application to amend the Particulars of Allegation in the
manner he requested.

Application for Some Parts of the Hearing to be heard in Private
31.
Mr Thomas made an application for parts of the evidence to be heard in private under Rule
39 of the Rules. He submitted that this was unlikely to be necessary in connection with
particulars 1 and 3 of the Allegation but might be relevant when evidence and submissions
were to be heard in connection with particular 2.

32.
The Committee took into account that subject to exceptions, Rule 39 requires that hearings of
the Committee must be heard in public. However, by Rule 39(3) (b), a hearing may be heard
wholly or partly in private if the Committee “is satisﬁed that the interests of the [Registrant]
in maintaining their privacy outweighs the public interest in holding the hearing, or part of
the hearing, in public”.

33.
It was of the view that it would be appropriate, if reference to the Registrant’s health is made
during the hearing, for those parts of the hearing to be heard in private.

13

Informing the Registrant of the Committee’s Decision to Proceed
34.
After the Committee decided to proceed with the hearing, and preliminary matters including
whether to hear health matters in private had been decided, the Committee Secretary wrote
to the Registrant in the following terms:

“Dear [Registrant],
The Committee has made a decision not to postpone and the hearing has started and will
continue in public except where there is mention of your health – that will be private. I will
provide their written decision with reasoning as soon as it becomes available.
If you wish to participate in the proceedings in any way going forward please do let me know.
Otherwise I will keep you updated as best I can.
Thank you”.

35.
The Registrant made no further contact with the Council thereafter.

Background, according to the Council
36.
The allegations reﬂect three concerns in chronological order. Throughout the period of
January 2023 to December 2024 the Registrant worked as the Responsible Pharmacist, at
Oakley Pharmacy in Heswell, Wirral (“the Pharmacy”).

Allegation 1

37.
The Council alleged that the Registrant failed to have in place or keep up to date a Controlled
Drugs Register, as required for Schedule 2 controlled drugs, when he plainly knew that such
controlled drugs were being supplied by the Pharmacy. There are two sources of information
in relation to this allegation.

38.
Mr O was a locum pharmacist who sometimes worked at the Pharmacy between January
and August 2023. He describes how it became apparent to him that Controlled Drugs
Registers were not being kept up to date or at all. He challenged the Registrant about this
and threatened to cancel his shifts in March 2023 unless the situation was remedied.

14

Despite some new software (Pharmsmart) being used on a trial basis, problems with the
CD registers persisted and Mr O parted ways with the Pharmacy in August 2023. He
produces text exchanges with the Registrant to illustrate how he raised his concerns and
the Registrant’s responses.

39.
The second source of information in relation to CD registers is the Council’s (former)
Inspector Mr L, who visited the Pharmacy in October 2023. On 9 October 2023 the Pharmacy
did not have a CD register available. However, by 11 October 2023 an electronic register had
been put in place. Dispensing data for controlled drugs was obtained from the Pharmacy
(from the Registrant) by the Council’s case oﬃcer in March 2024. These records cover the
period from January to October 2023. They appear in an Excel workbook with patient
identifying data redacted. The data was shown to the Inspector, Mr L, who undertook an
audit and reports that “several hundred supplies were made of Schedule 2 controlled drugs
that were not entered into a controlled drug (CD) register as received or supplies, in
accordance with the Misuse of Drugs Regulations”.

40.
In an email to the case oﬃcer on 18 April 2024, the Registrant replied “no” when asked if he
(or any other Pharmacy staﬀ) raised concerns to the then Superintendent in relation to
managing controlled drugs and ensuring accurate record keeping of controlled drugs.

41.
In his report from the Inspection on 11 October 2023 Mr L also noted that the Responsible
Pharmacist log was incomplete “with several dates between March 2023 and the inspection
date having no record to identify the pharmacist in duty when the pharmacy was trading. And
there was no RP record available prior to March 2023. This meant the pharmacy was not able
to demonstrate who was responsible at speciﬁc times”. Mr L had secured a hard copy of the
RP log which was before the Committee. This related to allegation 1.1.

15

Allegation 2

42.
On 27 September 2024, the Registrant was working as Responsible Pharmacist at the
Pharmacy. A concern was raised with a GP practice that occupies the same site as the
Pharmacy. This led to two witnesses from the surgery (Dr M and Ms K) speaking to the
Registrant and observing his presentation. Dr M was a GP partner at the practice. Ms K was
the practice manager. They spoke to the Registrant in person, individually and together.

43.
According to Dr M, the Registrant had “appeared drunk was unsteady on his feet when
walking round and slurring his words”. His breath smelt of mints. The Registrant denied that
he had been drinking but declined to take a breathalyser test (which the surgery had on
site). According to Ms K, when she ﬁrst saw the Registrant he was “sat in his chair
slumped”. When questioned about slurring his speech, the Registrant said that he was
getting used to (REDACTED). Ms K considered that he looked (REDACTED)

44.
(REDACTED)

Allegation 3

45.
On 12 December 2024, one of the Council’s inspectors, Mr W, was contacted by a park
ranger for Wirral Council (Mr S) about some dumped waste recovered from a park in
Heswall. The waste had been collected and moved to a separate location. Mr W attended
this site and made a search of the items, which had been stored in a bin. Photographs
appear in the bundle, and a list of items is found at paragraph 7 of the Inspector’s statement.
These items include zolpidem and lorazepam, which are schedule 4, part 1 controlled drugs.
The items also included one of Mr W’s business cards and other material that enabled him to
connect the waste with the Registrant’s pharmacy.

46.
In addition to this witness evidence, the Council also produces email correspondence
between the Inspector and Mr S in which further details and photographs are provided
illustrating how the dumped waste came to be found and what condition it was in before

16

being moved. For completeness, the dumped waste appears to include empty bottles of
alcohol. Further email contact took place between Mr s and the Council’s case oﬃcer.

47.
The concerns about pharmacy waste were put to the Registrant by the Council’s case oﬃcer,
by email, on 7 April 2025. In reply on 13 April 2025, the Registrant stated among other
things:

“I was responsible for leaving the items in the woods. Unfortunately (REDACTED).”

48.
One of the items recovered was a printed email correspondence between the Registrant and
one of the Council’s case oﬃcers. This would further link the Registrant with the actual
dumping of the waste. According to Google Maps, the park where the waste was found is
less that one mile from the Pharmacy premises (270 Telegraph Road).

49.
The Inspector explains in his statement how the controlled drugs had to be taken to a local
pharmacy for secure disposal. The recovered waste included other prescription-only drugs
(e.g. amoxicillin) which could have been misused if recovered by a member of the public.
The waste also included a near miss log with pharmacy staﬀ details.

Registrant’s Response
50.
The Registrant provided no formal response to the Particulars of Allegation, nor did he
provide any evidence in relation to the concerns nor in relation to any insight or remediation.

51.
However, the ﬁle note of Ms Raimundova, the Committee Secretary, in relation to a phone
conversation she had with the Registrant on 24 June 2026, set out that she read him the
allegations (as drafted prior to their subsequent amendment at the start of this hearing),
because he said he had not read them before, and then:

“I asked [the Registrant] whether he would wish to send any response to the allegations, or
attend to address the Committee directly. He said ‘No, because they are correct’. I asked
whether it means that he would have admitted to those allegations and he said yes”.

17

DETERMINATION ON THE FACTS

52.
The Committee then turned to make its determination in relation to the alleged facts in the
ﬁrst instance.

53.
In reaching its decisions on facts, the Committee considered the documentation listed at the
start of this determination, and the submissions made by Mr Thomas on behalf of the
Council. Mr Thomas told the Committee that this was not a case in which it should give itself
a “good character” direction – in any case such a direction would only apply to propensity,
and not to credibility since there was no signiﬁcant evidence provided by the Registrant in
relation to the concerns.

54.
When considering each particular of allegation, the Committee bore in mind that the burden
of proof rests on the Council and that particulars are found proved based on the balance of
probabilities. This means that particulars will be proved if the Committee is satisﬁed that
what is alleged is more likely than not to have happened.

55.
The Committee was of the view that all of the live witnesses did their best to assist the
Committee and were open and honest.

56.
It noted however that Mr L, the Council’s Inspector at the time, had not appeared to recall,
when giving live evidence to the Committee, that he had been copied into emails which the
Registrant had sent to the Council attaching extracts of electronic CD registers which were
before the Committee. It noted that the Registrant sent the emails with attachments to the
Council between 18-24 March 2025, sometime after the two dates on which Mr L attended
the Pharmacy, 9 and 11 October 2023, when, according to Mr L, there was no CD register
available on 9 October but there was an electronic register present on 11 October 2023.

18

Particular 1 and the stem of the Allegation

“You, a registered pharmacist, being the Responsible Pharmacist at Oakley Pharmacy,
270 Telegraph Road, Heswall, Wirral CH60 7SE (“the pharmacy”),

1. Between January 2023 and October 2023, failed to:
1.1 keep an up-to-date Responsible Pharmacist record
1.2 have in place and/or keep up to date a controlled drugs register when you knew or
ought to have known that the pharmacy was dispensing controlled drugs

57.
The evidence in support of this allegation included the audit of the Responsible Pharmacist
(“RP”) record for the relevant period; the audit of what was available from the digital
Controlled Drugs Register for the relevant period together with the Excel spread sheet
demonstrating the supply of controlled drugs made by the Pharmacy during that period; and
the witness evidence of Mr O who was a locum pharmacist working part time at the
Pharmacy.

58.
In relation to sub-particular 1.1, the Committee observed that the audit of the RP record for
the relevant dates showed that there were a number of dates in which there was no entry at
all indicating that an RP was present, although the evidence from Mr L was that the
Pharmacy was opened at least five days a week and also possibly at weekends. Moreover, on
the majority of occasions set out in the audit, where an RP had registered an entry in the
morning, there was no corresponding time entered for when the RP would have terminated
their duty on that day. The Committee noted that this absence of an entry showing the time
of termination applied not only to entries by the Registrant but also those by the witness Mr
O and other RPs.

59.
Whilst the evidence suggested that the RP record had not been kept up to date, there was no
evidence before the Committee of any instances when the Registrant was in fact present as
an RP but had not recorded this. The Committee observed that the Registrant was neither
the Superintendent at the relevant time, (he became the Superintendent later on 14

19

November 2023), nor was he alleged to have been the owner of the Pharmacy. In these
circumstances, the Committee was of the view that the Council had not discharged its
burden to prove that the Registrant had a professional duty to keep the RP record up to date
generally, including in relation to other RPs. Therefore, it could not be said that the
Registrant had “failed” to keep an up-to-date Responsible Pharmacist record.

60.
The Committee noted, in fairness, that Mr Thomas had made what he called a “realistic
concession” in closing submissions on the facts, that the Council’s evidence in support of this
allegation was now somewhat weak.

61.
The Committee found sub-particular 1.1 not proved.

62.
As for sub-particular 1.2, the Committee carefully considered the evidence. Mr Thomas had
submitted that the evidence was from two main sources: Mr L who inspected the Pharmacy
in October 2023; and Mr O who was a locum pharmacist for some of the relevant time.

63.
Mr L had stated in his Investigation Report of 11 October 2023 that the Superintendent had
resigned on 23 September 2023, and the Pharmacy was operating without a nominated
superintendent. His evidence from the inspection was that there was evidence that Schedule
2 controlled drugs were being dispensed and supplied by the Pharmacy but were not entered
into CD registers as was required by law. Staff at the Pharmacy were unsure whether the CD
registers were being kept up to date and it appeared that they thought the Registrant was
responsible for doing so.

64.
The Inspection Report recorded that:

“At the time of inspection, an electronic CD register was in place and entries had been made
for four strengths of Methylphenidate XL. But no other electronic CD records had been made”.

There were also some old paper records dating from April 2021.

20

65.
The Committee noted however that Mr L’s Inspection report had been written in October
2023, some months before March 2024 when the Registrant had sent a number of electronic
CD records to the Council, copying Mr L in.

66.
Taking the above into account, and having heard Mr L’s live evidence, the Committee was
not satisfied that he had taken account of the CD records sent in by the Registrant in March
2024, when he came to the conclusion that the records were not kept up to date. He did not
appear to recall seeing those records, when asked about them in live evidence. The
Committee could not therefore rely on Mr L’s assessment of the state of the CD recording as
set out in his Inspection Record.

67.
As for the evidence of Mr O, there was clear documentary evidence in the form of messages
on text that Mr O was concerned about the lack of CD record-keeping whilst he was working
at the Pharmacy as a locum between March and August 2023. He told the Committee that he
asked the Registrant informally a number of times, to deal with his concern, but later he
decided to be more formal and record his concerns in texts. He would receive repeated
assurances from the Registrant that the matter was being dealt with.

68.
For example, in March 2023, the following exchange took place:

20 March 2023

THE COMMITTEE’S DECISION ON GROUNDS AND IMPAIRMENT

98.
Having found particulars 2 and 3 proved in their entirety, the Committee then went on to the
second stage of the proceedings, that is, to determine whether or not the Registrant’s fitness
to practise is currently impaired. It took into account the relevant law including case law and
also took into account the submissions of Mr Thomas on behalf of the Council.

99.
Article 54(1) of the Pharmacy Order 2010 provides:

“The Fitness to Practise Committee must determine whether or not the ﬁtness to practise of
the person in respect of whom the allegation is made (referred to in this article as “the person
concerned”) is impaired”.

28

100.
The Council has set out the meaning of ‘ﬁtness to practise’ in its guidance entitled: “Good
decision-making: Fitness to practise Hearings and Outcomes Guidance” (Revised March
2024). Paragraph 2.12 states:
“2.12 A pharmacy professional is ‘ﬁt to practise’ when they have the skills, knowledge,
character, behaviour and health needed to work as a pharmacist or pharmacy technician
safely and eﬀectively. In practical terms, this means maintaining appropriate standards of
competence, demonstrating good character, and also keeping to the principles of good
practice set out in our various standards, guidance and advice.”

101.
Consideration of impairment is undertaken in two stages. First, the Committee has to
consider whether, on the facts found proved, there has been misconduct. It then has to
consider whether, as a result, the Registrant’s ﬁtness to practise is currently impaired. This
approach was outlined by Mr Justice Cranston at paragraph 19 of Cheatle v GMC [2009]
EWHC 645 (Admin):
“A Panel must engage in a 2-step process. First, it must decide whether there has been
misconduct, deficient professional performance or whether the other circumstances set out in the
section are present. Then it must go on to determine whether, as a result, fitness to practise is
impaired. But it may be that despite a [practitioner] having been guilty of misconduct, for
example, a Panel may decide that his or her fitness to practise is not impaired.

Evidence at Stage 2
102.

the Registrant’s previous regulatory history. He provided the Committee with the following
documents:

• FTP Committee Determination from September 2019 (Principal Hearing)
• FTP Committee Determination from March 2023 (Principal Hearing Review)
• FTP Committee Determination from May 2025 (Interim Order Review).

29

to (REDACTED). The Conditions were renewed and extended twice and then, in March 2023,

concerns. The Committee’s determination sets out that on that occasion the Registrant said
“(REDACTED)”

The Committee’s Decision

Grounds
107.
Article 51(1) of the Order set out the possible grounds or “gateways” to a ﬁnding of
impairment. The relevant gateway in this matter is:

• “misconduct” (Article 51(1)(a)).

108.
The Committee turned to consider whether the facts it had found proved amount to the
ground of misconduct.

109.
The Committee ﬁrst considered the facts proved in light of the Council’s Standards for
Pharmacy Professionals (May 2017).

110.
It was of the view that the Registrant breached the following Standards:
- Standard 5 – Pharmacy professionals must use their professional judgement
- Standard 6 – Pharmacy professionals must behave in a professional manner
- Standard 7 – Pharmacy professionals must respect and maintain a person’s
conﬁdentiality and privacy
- Standard 8 – Pharmacy professionals must speak up when they have concerns or when
things go wrong
- Standard 9 – Pharmacy professionals must demonstrate leadership

111.
Dealing ﬁrst with the Registrant’s proven conduct at particular 2, the Committee
considered that the Registrant failed to use his professional judgement and to work in a
professional manner, by attending work whilst unﬁt, and having consumed alcohol,
instead of removing himself from the pharmacy workplace or seeking help. His conduct in
attending work whilst unﬁt to do so struck at the core of the fundamental responsibility of
a pharmacist to ensure he can safely and eﬀectively carry out his responsibilities, which,
on 27 September 2024, given the evidence of witnesses, the Registrant would have been
quite unable to do. Whilst there was no evidence that he had in fact made errors on duty,

31

it was, the Committee considered, extremely irresponsible of the Registrant to attempt to
work whilst unﬁt; and particularly so given his previous regulatory history. This was not
the ﬁrst time the Registrant had been at work whilst unﬁt, having consumed alcohol, and
so he should have been well aware of the professional implications and the implications
for patient safety of doing so. The fact that he was in a position of seniority as RP made
such conduct even more serious; he failed to show leadership and he failed to speak up
when things were going wrong.

112.
Turning to the Registrant’s conduct at particular 3, the Committee accepted the submissions
of Mr Thomas to the eﬀect that the disposal of pharmacy waste in bin bags in the
undergrowth of a public park showed very poor judgement, a lack of professionalism, and a
disregard for conﬁdentiality in that some of the documents included staﬀ details, as well as
details of the Council’s Inspector and case oﬃcer. Disposing of waste in this way also would
have presented a burden on park users, volunteers and rangers.

113.
The Registrant’s conduct in particular 3 would, the Committee considered, also have posed a
serious risk to the public. Recklessly dumping medication including prescription drugs and
controlled drugs in plastic bags in a local park, undermined the very safeguards designed to
protect patients and the public; anyone could have found the drugs and used them or
diverted them to be used by others.

114.
The Committee bore in mind that the Standards may be taken into account when considering
the issues of grounds and impairment but that a breach of the Standards does not
automatically result in a ﬁnding of misconduct (Rule 24(11) of the Rules).

115.
However, given the proven facts of this case, the Committee was satisﬁed that the
Registrant’s conduct individually and collectively fell short of what would be proper in the
circumstances. It was of the view that his conduct would be regarded as deplorable by fellow
practitioners and would convey a degree of opprobrium to the ordinary citizen. His behaviour
was, in the words of the recent case of Forz Khan v Bar Standards Board [2018] EWHC 2184
(Admin), "seriously reprehensible".

32

116.
The Committee therefore determined that the Registrant’s conduct was serious enough to
amount to professional misconduct.

Impairment
117.
The Committee went on to consider whether the Registrant’s ﬁtness to practise is currently
impaired.

118.
Rule 5(2) of the Rules provides:

“In relation to evidence about the conduct or behaviour of the registrant which might cast
doubt on whether the requirements as to ﬁtness to practise are met in relation to the
registrant, the Committee must have regard to whether or not that conduct or behaviour –

a) presents an actual or potential risk to patients or to the public;
b) has brought, or might being, the profession of pharmacy into disrepute;
c) has breached one of the fundamental principles of the profession of
pharmacy; or
d) shows that the integrity of the registrant can no longer be relied upon.”

119.
Guidance on this issue was set out by Mr Justice Silber in Cohen v General Medical Council
[2008] EWHC 581 (Admin) at paragraph 65:

“It must be highly relevant in determining if a [practitioner’s] fitness to practise is impaired
that first … her conduct that led to the charge is easily remediable, second that it has been
remedied and third that it is highly unlikely to be repeated”.

120.
These principles are echoed in the Council’s “Good decision making: Fitness to practise
hearings and outcomes guidance (2024) at paragraph 2.15:

33

“The committee should also consider whether:
• the conduct which led to the complaint is able to be addressed
• the conduct which led to the complaint has been addressed
• the conduct which led to the complaint is likely to be repeated
• a finding of impairment is needed to declare and uphold proper standards of behaviour
and/or maintain public confidence in the profession”.

121.
The Committee took into account the information before it relevant to the question of
current impairment. This included the evidence of previous regulatory ﬁndings connected
with the Registrant’s long-standing history of alcohol dependency. Most recently on 23 June
2026 the Registrant had emailed Mr Thomas stating that all of his conduct as alleged by the
Council was due to (REDACTED.)

122.
The Committee noted that this was a case based on the ground of misconduct, but the
evidence before it was that the misconduct could have followed on from (REDACTED).

123.
Turning to consider whether the Registrant’s ﬁtness to practise is currently impaired as at
today’s date, the Committee observed that the Registrant had not attended this hearing, and
he had provided no submissions nor any information on the basis of which it could have
assessed the Registrant’s insight or reﬂections upon his failings, or whether he has in any
respect remediated his conduct.

124.
It took into account the comments the Registrant made at the interim order hearing in May
2025 which Mr Thomas had drawn to its attention, which, it considered did demonstrate a
degree of insight about the current concerns.

125.
The Registrant had told the Committee then that the concerns alleged were due to
(REDACTED.) The Determination continued:

“He expressed that he was disappointed with himself, but stated that he was now
sober….When the Committee asked questions about any risk he represented to patients safety

34

he stated that he was (REDACTED.)

126.
The Registrant had provided no evidence to this Committee however, (REDACTED). The
Committee could not therefore ﬁnd that the Registrant’s conduct has as at the date of this
hearing, been addressed.

127.
As for whether the conduct is likely to be repeated, the Committee observed that whether or
not the Registrant’s misconduct took place against (REDACTED), this was nevertheless a
Registrant in a responsible position as RP, with a previous very similar regulatory ﬁnding
against him amounting to misconduct due to attending work whilst unﬁt to do so. This was

128.
In these circumstances, the Committee has concluded that, on the basis of the evidence
before it, the Registrant’s conduct is likely to be repeated.

129.
The Committee next turned to consider its ﬁndings in light of Rule 5(2) of the Rules. It
accepted Mr Thomas’s submissions that three limbs of Rule (5)(2), namely, (a), (b) and (c) are
engaged by the Registrant’s conduct.

Rule 5(2)(a)

130.
The Registrant’s conduct demonstrates behaviour that presents both an actual and potential
risk to the public. Attending work whilst unﬁt to do so, having drunk alcohol, and especially in
the senior role of RP on the day, clearly challenged the Registrant’s ability to act responsibly
and safely in a professional context. It presented a risk that he might make errors of
judgement or simply abdicate responsibility (the Committee noted that the Pharmacy
Incident Report recorded that the Registrant went to “rest in the oﬃce for a while” because

35

(REDACTED)). Given the Committee’s ﬁnding that the risk of repetition is high, there remains
a potential risk in future.

Rule 5(2)(b)

131.
Pharmacy professionals are expected to attend work only when ﬁt to do so and to dispose of
potentially dangerous medications safely in accordance with regulatory guidance. The
Registrant’s conduct clearly was incompatible with that. His misconduct had the potential to
diminish public trust and conﬁdence in the profession and brought the entire profession of
pharmacy into disrepute.

Rule 5(2)(c)

132.
Fundamental principles of the profession of pharmacy include attending work only when ﬁt
to do so – because there are obvious risks to patient and public safety if they attend work
unﬁt – and also disposing of medication safely and securely. The Registrant breached both
those principles by his misconduct.

Rule 5(2)(d)

133.
The Committee carefully considered whether the Registrant’s integrity can no longer be
relied on. As Mr Thomas had submitted, although it might be said that the Registrant’s actions
fell far below what a pharmacist acting with integrity would have done, this was a case in which it
should question carefully whether or not the character of the misconduct, given the backdrop in
relation to (REDACTED) is akin to a lack of integrity.

134.
The Committee took into account that the Registrant had a previous regulatory finding against him
for misconduct in attending work whilst unfit to do so, coupled with a finding of (REDACTED.) He had
not been open and honest with colleagues and the staff of the nearby GP surgery on 27 September
2024 when he denied that he had been using alcohol on that day.

36

135.
It also noted that the Committee at the Principal Hearing set out that he was given a Warning by the
Council’s Investigation Committee in 2012 for two occasions on which he did not notify the Council
of convictions for drink driving offences which he received in 2005 and 2008.

136.
(REDACTED)

137.
On the other hand, the Registrant had admitted (after a few weeks) that he was responsible for the
disposal of the medication and confidential waste in the park when asked about it by the Council’s
case officer; and he had admitted both in the IOR hearing and in an email to a Council case officer in
May 2025, and very recently in his email to Mr Thomas, that his conduct then alleged was due to a
(REDACTED.) Whilst he had not made formal admissions to the particulars, he appeared to have
accepted that, for the most part, he had behaved as alleged.

138.
Although the facts found proved are very serious, and the Registrant very clearly knew better, having
gone through a previous regulatory process for similar conduct, and having received a regulatory
Warning prior to that, there is compelling evidence before it that the Registrant’s misconduct
occurred (REDACTED)

139.
In these circumstances the Committee has concluded that Rule 5(2) (d) is not currently engaged.

140.
Turning lastly to consider the public interest, the Committee bore in mind the well- known
case of CHRE v NMC and Grant [EWHC] 927 (Admin), in which Mrs Justice Cox stated that a
panel must consider whether “the need to uphold proper professional standards and public
conﬁdence in the profession would be undermined if a ﬁnding of impairment were not made
in the particular circumstances” of a case.

141.
The Committee was satisﬁed that this case is clearly one, given its facts, in which there is a
need to make a ﬁnding of current impairment in order to declare and uphold proper
standards of behaviour and maintain public conﬁdence in the profession.

142.
For all the reasons set out above, the Committee ﬁnds the Registrant’s ﬁtness to practise is

37

currently impaired on grounds of public protection and otherwise in the public interest, that
is, in order to promote and maintain public conﬁdence in the professions regulated by the
Council; and to promote and maintain proper professional standards and conduct for
members of those professions.

Decision on Outcome
143.
Having found impairment, the Committee went on to consider the appropriate outcome.

144.
The Committee’s powers in relation to sanction are set out in Article 54(2) of the Pharmacy
Order 2010.

145.
Article 54(2) of the Order provides:

“If the Fitness to Practise Committee determines that the person concerned’s ﬁtness to
practise is impaired, it may–

a. give a warning to the person concerned in connection with any matter arising out of or
related to the allegation and give a direction that details of the warning must be
recorded in the person concerned’s entry in the register,
b. give advice to any other person or other body involved in the investigation of the
allegation on any issue arising out of or related to the allegation;
c. give a direction that the person concerned be removed from the register;
d. give a direction that the entry in the Register of the person concerned be suspended,
for such period not exceeding 12 months as may be speciﬁed in the directions; or
e. give a direction that the entry in the Register person of the person concerned be
conditional upon that person complying, during such period not exceeding 3 years as
may be speciﬁed in the direction, with such requirements speciﬁed in the direction as
the Committee thinks ﬁt to impose for the protection of the public or otherwise in the
public interest or in the interest of the person concerned.”

The Committee may also make no order.

38

146.
The Committee was aware that it should consider the available outcomes in ascending order
from the least restrictive, taking no action, to the most restrictive, removal from the register,
in order to identify the appropriate and proportionate outcome that meets the circumstances
of this case. It bore in mind that the purpose of the outcome is not to be punitive, though an
outcome may in fact have a punitive eﬀect. The purpose of the outcome is to meet the
overarching objectives of regulation, namely the protection of the public, the maintenance of
public conﬁdence and to promote and uphold professional standards. The Committee is
therefore entitled to give greater weight to the public interest over the Registrant’s interests.

147.
The Committee had regard to the GPhC’s guidance, entitled: Good decision making: Fitness
to practise hearings and outcomes guidance (March 2024), (“the Good decision making
Guidance”) which reminds the Committee that it must consider the full range of outcomes.

Submissions on behalf of the Council

148.
Mr Thomas provided the Committee with documentation relating to the Warning imposed
on the Registrant by the Council’s Investigating Committee in 2012. He submitted that this
dates from events which took place nearly 20 years ago and the Committee should not take
it into account in deciding on outcome but could bear it in mind when considering the
background context regarding the Registrant’s (REDACTED)

149.
He proposed a number of aggravating and mitigating factors which the Committee should
take into account and also referred to the fact that the Registrant has been suspended from
practicing for about 19 months and this might also be relevant when the Committee
considers proportionality of any potential outcome. He submitted that though this is not a
health case and therefore it is open to the Committee to impose an outcome of removal, the
Council’s submission was that a period of 8-10 months with a review might be the
appropriate outcome in this case.

39

The Committee’s Decision

150.
The Committee had regard to the relevant law and to the Council’s ‘Good decision
making: Fitness to practise hearings and outcomes guidance (March 2024)’ (“the
Good decision making Guidance”), to inform its decision. It took into account the
submissions made by Mr Thomas and all of the relevant documentation.

151.
The Committee ﬁrst considered what, if any, aggravating and mitigating factors there
may be.

152.
The Committee identiﬁed the following aggravating factors:
• The Registrant has a regulatory history including an IC Warning dating from 2012 for
not having informed the Council of two separate convictions for drink driving
offences; and findings at a Principal Hearing in 2019 relating to attending work whilst
unfit to do so and an (REDACTED);
• Given the above, the Registrant would have known about the regulatory
consequences of his conduct;
• Whilst there was no evidence of patient or public harm, the Registrant’s conduct in
relation to the facts proved both individually and together could have caused serious
harm to patients and the public;

153.
The Committee identiﬁed the following mitigating factors:

• The misconduct is said by the Registrant to have (REDACTED)

• No evidence of actual harm to patients or the public;
• No confidential patient details were found discarded in the park;
• The Registrant accepted that he should leave the Pharmacy when asked to do so
by Dr M;

40

• The Registrant admitted that he had discarded the waste in the park; and admitted
that he (REDACTED).

154.
The Committee next turned to consider the sanctions or outcomes available to it in
ascending order.

155.
Take no Action: The Committee ﬁrst considered where it would be appropriate to
take no action, however it was of the view that this outcome would not protect the
public nor would it be suﬃcient to reﬂect the seriousness of the Registrant’s
misconduct.

156.
Warning: The Committee next considered whether issuing a Warning would be
appropriate but it decided that a Warning would not be appropriate for the same
reasons as above, namely that a Warning would not protect the public nor
suﬃciently mark the public interest, because, in the Committee’s view, a Warning
would not be proportionate to the seriousness of the Registrant’s failings.

157.
Conditions of Practice. The Committee next considered whether to impose
conditions of practice. The Good decision making guidance states that conditions
may be appropriate where there is evidence of poor performance, or signiﬁcant
shortcomings in a professional’s practice, but the Committee is satisﬁed that the
professional may respond positively to retraining and supervision; and where there is
not a signiﬁcant risk posed to the public by the imposition of conditions.

158.
However this was not a case in which the Registrant’s standard of professional
practice was called into question – moreover, though the misconduct may be said to
have taken place during the course of the Registrant’s practice, and his past
regulatory history demonstrates that he has in the past complied with conditions
including undergoing substance use tests, he has not engaged with this regulatory
matter in any meaningful way since June 2025. The Committee cannot therefore be
assured that he would abide by any conditions it might consider appropriate to deal
with the misconduct it has found proved.

41

159.
In any event, the Committee is of the view an order for conditions would not be
suﬃcient to mark the seriousness of the matter and send a clear message to the
Registrant’s professional colleagues and to the public that his conduct was
unacceptable for a registered professional, so as to maintain public conﬁdence in the
profession and the regulator.

160.
Suspension Order. The Committee next considered whether suspension would be a
proportionate sanction.

161.
It took into account that Mr Thomas had submitted, on behalf of the Council, that
suspension would be an appropriate and proportionate outcome in this case, given
the evidence that the Registrant’s misconduct may have occurred against the
backdrop of (REDACTED.)

162.
The Committee carefully considered the Council’s Good decision making guidance
which indicates that suspension may be appropriate where:
“The Committee considers that a warning or conditions are not suﬃcient to
deal with any risk to patient safety or to protect the public, or would
undermine public conﬁdence. When it is necessary to highlight to the
profession and the public that the conduct of the professional is unacceptable
and unbeﬁtting a member of the pharmacy profession. Also when public
conﬁdence in the profession demands no lesser outcome”.

163.
The Committee took into account that the Council’s Good decision making guidance
states at paragraph 5.7 and 5.8 that in reaching a decision on what outcome to
impose, the Committee should give appropriate weight to the wider public interest.
The Committee is entitled to give greater weight to the public interest, than to the
consequences for the professional. Even if an outcome will have a punitive eﬀect, it
may still be appropriate.

42

164.
The Committee is satisﬁed that patients and members of the public would be
appropriately protected during the period of any suspension of the Registrant’s name
from the register. It was also of the view that a period of suspension might assist the
Registrant to gather evidence of (REDACTED) and provide appropriate material
demonstrating insight and remediation for his misconduct which he might present to
a committee at a review.

165.
It therefore turned to consider whether a suspension would be adequate and
proportionate to maintain public conﬁdence in the profession and proper standards
of behaviour.

166.
In deciding on the appropriate and proportionate outcome, the Committee bore in
mind that this case had been brought by the Council on the ground of misconduct,
(REDACTED). However, the Committee took full account of the evidence which the
Council had fairly brought to the Committee’s attention, which suggested that the
Registrant may have been (REDACTED.)

167.
(REDACTED)

168.
The Committee noted however that there appeared to have been only a relatively
short period between the date he was returned to the register unrestricted (Principal
Hearing Review in March 2023), and the (REDACTED.) The Registrant had provided no
independent information to this Committee which might support what he had told
the Interim Order Review committee in May 2025 to the eﬀect that he was, then,
“sober”. This Committee has no evidence from the Registrant about (REDACTED.)

169.
Taking all the above into account, the Committee has, after careful consideration,
concluded that it is fair to impose a period of suspension on the Registrant’s right to
practise, together with a review before its end, in the hope that he can use this
period to (REDACTED), and gather together the evidence which a reviewing
committee will need to see in order to assess his ﬁtness to practise at the date of any
such review.

43

170.
It is of the view that a suspension with a review will satisfactorily mark the
seriousness and nature of its ﬁndings, and that members of the public, were they to
be appraised of all the evidence in this case, would consider such an outcome to be
appropriate, reasonable and fair.

171.
The Committee concluded that the suspension should be for the longest period
available, that is, 12 months, which will be proportionate to the seriousness of the
concerns, and also may give the Registrant suﬃcient time to prepare for the review.

172.
The Committee wishes to emphasise that as this is a case where serious misconduct
has been found, removal from the register remains an option for the committee at
the review. Given the Registrant’s previous regulatory history, that may be an
appropriate outcome at the ﬁrst review if he is not able to demonstrate full, or at
least signiﬁcant steps towards, appropriate insight and remediation in relation to the
serious failings found proved by this Committee.

173.
The Committee hereby revokes the Interim Order of Suspension in this matter.

174.
As stated above, the Committee considers that this is a case in which a review will be
necessary before the expiry of the suspension. The reviewing committee would be
assisted by the Registrant providing the following:

i)
The Registrant’s attendance at any review;

ii)
A reﬂective document demonstrating the Registrant’s full insight into the
seriousness of his misconduct, explaining that he understands what he should
have done at the time and what he would do in future to avoid repeating his
failings. He should set out his insight into and understanding of the risk to
public protection and to the wider public interest;

44

iii)
Any testimonials he can provide about any work he has undertaken whether
paid or voluntary;

175.
Removal. Having concluded that a period of suspension would satisfactorily deal with
the issues of public protection and public interest which it has identiﬁed, the
Committee considered whether removal was in fact more appropriate. The
Committee took into account that removal is reserved for the most serious conduct.
The Good decision making Guidance states that:
“Removing a professional’s registration is reserved for the most serious
conduct… The committee should consider this outcome when the
professional’s behaviour is fundamentally incompatible with being a
registered professional”.

176.
Taking all of the evidence into account, the Committee has come to the view that the
Registrant’s conduct is not fundamentally incompatible with being a registered
professional and therefore removal of his name from the register would be
disproportionate.

177.
The Committee therefore directs that the entry in the Register of Mr Jitendra Desai
whose registration number is 2048785, be suspended from the register for a period
of 12 months.

45

Decision on Interim Measure
178.
Mr Thomas made an application for an interim measure of suspension to be imposed
on the Registrant’s registration, pursuant to Article 60 of the Pharmacy Order 2010,
pending the coming into force of the Committee’s substantive order. He submitted
that such an order was necessary to protect the public and was otherwise in the
public interest.

179.
The Committee carefully considered the Council’s application. It took account of the
fact that its decision to order the suspension of the Registrant’s name from the
register will not take effect until 28 days after the Registrant is formally notified of
the outcome, or until any appeal is concluded. The Committee also took into account
the Council’s Good Decision-making: Hearings and Outcomes Guidance of 2024.

180.
The Committee has found that the Registrant’s conduct merits an order of
suspension because it considers there is a high risk of repetition and an order of
suspension is therefore necessary for public protection and is also in the public
interest.

181.
The Committee is satisfied that it is therefore necessary for an interim measure of
suspension to be in place from today’s date, both because it is necessary to protect
the public from potential harm should the Registrant repeat his conduct, and also
otherwise in the public interest, to uphold proper professional standards and
maintain confidence in the profession and the Regulator.

182.
The Committee therefore hereby orders that the entry of the Registrant in the
register be suspended forthwith, both on grounds of public protection and in the
public interest, pending the coming into force of the substantive order.
